classification.habitat: Humid tropical evergreen settings; grown in plantations and home gardens on well-drained soils.
classification.distribution: Native to the Moluccas; cultivated in India mainly in Kerala, Tamil Nadu and parts of Karnataka and Assam.

identification.description: Ovoid hard seed with marbled/ruminate brown endosperm and strong characteristic aromatic odor; mace is the separate aril.
identification.whole_plant: Dioecious (occasionally monoecious) aromatic evergreen tree, about 10–20 m high, with dense conical crown.
identification.stem: Erect trunk with greyish-brown smooth bark; branches spreading, exuding reddish sap when cut.
identification.leaf: Simple, alternate, elliptic to oblong-lanceolate, glossy dark green above, paler below, aromatic when crushed.
identification.flower: Small, pale yellow, urn-shaped unisexual flowers in axillary umbellate clusters; perianth 3-lobed.
identification.fruit: Fleshy, pear-shaped to globose yellow drupe-like fruit that splits into two valves to expose the seed covered by a crimson lacinate aril (mace, Jatipatri).
identification.seed: Seed (kernel) ellipsoid, 20–30 mm long and about 20 mm broad, greenish-brown and reticulately furrowed outside; cut surface shows dark brown ruminations of perisperm in greyish-brown endosperm; odour strong aromatic, taste pungent and aromatic.
identification.bark: Smooth, greyish-brown bark exuding a reddish juice when cut.
identification_points: Ellipsoid kernel, 2–3 cm long, reticulately furrowed
Strong aromatic odour and pungent taste
Crimson lacinate aril (mace) surrounds the fresh seed

useful_part: aril (Jatipatri is a separate drug part)
therapeutics.precautions: Use only in the recommended small dose; larger amounts of nutmeg are narcotic and can cause nausea, palpitations, dizziness and hallucinations. Being Ushna and Tikshna, it may aggravate Pitta.
therapeutics.contraindications: Pregnancy and lactation, young children, Pitta-predominant conditions and bleeding disorders; avoid with sedatives or psychoactive medicines.

shlokas:
जातीफलं जातिकोशं मालतीफलमित्यपि ।
जातीफलं रसे तिक्तं तीक्ष्णोष्णं रोचनं लघु ।
कटुकं दीपनं ग्राहि स्वर्यं श्लेष्मानिलापहम् ॥
निहन्ति मुखवैरस्यं मलदौर्गन्ध्यकृष्णताः ।
कृमिकासवमिश्वासशोषपीनसहृद्रुजः ॥
nighantu_references: Bhavaprakasha Nighantu, Karpuradi Varga, verses 48–49 in the searchable recension; numbering varies by edition.
classical_reference.shloka_reference_status: verified against searchable Bhavaprakasha text; supplied batch verse was corrected to the searchable recension

major_constituents: Essential oil (sabinene, alpha- and beta-pinene, myristicin, elemicin, safrole, eugenol)
Fixed oil (nutmeg butter, rich in trimyristin)
phytochemistry.chemical_notes: API lists essential oil and fixed oil; myristicin and elemicin in the volatile oil are responsible for the psychoactive toxicity of large doses.

modern_information.evidence_summary: Nutmeg is an aromatic stimulant used for improving digestion, inducing sleep, and relieving pain.
recognized_uses: Carminative and antidiarrhoeal in traditional systems
Source of nutmeg oil and nutmeg butter
modern_information.safety_notes: Nutmeg intoxication (anticholinergic-like symptoms, agitation, hallucinations, tachycardia) is reported after ingestion of several grams; keep doses within the pharmacopoeial range.

exam_points: Jatiphala = Myristica fragrans Houtt., family Myristicaceae
Useful part: seed kernel; aril is the separate drug Jatipatri (mace)
Rasa Tikta, Katu; Guna Laghu, Tikshna; Virya Ushna; Vipaka Katu
Karma: Deepana, Grahi, Rochana, Mukhadaurgandhyanashaka, Kaphavatahara
Indicated in Atisara, Grahani, Mukharoga, Kasa, Shwasa
Dose: churna 0.5–1 g; large doses are narcotic (myristicin)
viva_questions: What is the difference between Jatiphala and Jatipatri?
What gives the cut nutmeg its marbled appearance?
Why is the dose of Jatiphala kept small?
Name a formulation containing Jatiphala used in Atisara.
student.quick_revision: Nutmeg is an aromatic stimulant used for improving digestion, inducing sleep, and relieving pain.

teaching_points: Show one plant yielding two drugs: seed (Jatiphala) and aril (Jatipatri).
Link Grahi action to its use in Atisara and Grahani.
Explain dose-dependent toxicity using myristicin as an example.
discussion_points: Spice versus medicine: dose makes the difference
Ruminate endosperm as a diagnostic character
practical_points: Cut a kernel transversely and observe ruminations.
Compare the seed with mace and note colour and odour.

doctor.quick_reference: Jatiphala (Myristica fragrans seed): Ushna, Tikshna, Grahi and Deepana drug for Atisara, Grahani and Kapha-Vata disorders; 0.5–1 g churna.
key_precautions: Do not exceed 1 g churna; narcotic in large doses
Avoid in pregnancy and in children
